# Secure agentic workflows

@include 'alerts/enterprise-and-hcp.mdx'

Use Vault Enterprise and your ID provider to implement zero trust principles
with narrowly scoped agent credentials.

## Before you start

- **You must have a Vault Enterprise or HCP Vault Dedicated server deployed**.

- **You must configure a supported identity or OAuth provider**:

    - [Use IBM Verify for agent IAM](/vault/ai/iam/providers/verify)
    - [Use Entra ID for agent IAM](/vault/ai/iam/providers/entraid)
    - [Use Okta for agent IAM](/vault/ai/iam/providers/okta)
    - [Use Auth0 for agent IAM](/vault/ai/iam/providers/auth0)

- **You must have admin permissions on Vault**. You need a Vault token with
  sufficient ACL policies attached to configure and modify your Vault deployment.


## Step 1: Create an OAuth resource server profile

<Tabs>

<Tab heading="Verify" group="verify">

1. Create an OAuth resource server configuration file called `verify-oauth.json`
   using the environment variables you saved during provider setup:

    ```shell-session
    $ cat > verify-oauth.json << EOF
    {
      "issuer_id":            "${ISSUER}",
      "use_jwks":             true,
      "user_claim":           "sub",
      "supported_algorithms": ["RS256"],
      "jwks_uri":             "${JWKS_URI}"
    }
    EOF
    ```

    <Warning title="IBM Verify limitation">

    Avoid validating with the `audiences` value with Verify STS clients as the
    client performing the OBO token exchange with RAR authorization details
    does not support `audience` mapping in the access token mapping.

    </Warning>

1. Create an OAuth resource server profile using the JSON file:

    ```shell-session
    $ vault write sys/config/oauth-resource-server/verify @verify-oauth.json

    WARNING! The following warnings were returned from Vault:
    * algorithm "RS256" is functional but consider using PS256 (RSA-PSS) for
    better security
    * profile supports only one algorithm family - consider supporting multiple
    families for flexibility
    ```

1. Read the profile to check for correctness.

    ```shell-session
    $ vault read sys/config/oauth-resource-server/verify

    Key                     Value
    ---                     -----
    audiences               [https://localhost:8200/v1]
    clock_skew_leeway       0
    config_id               de81dc66-e00d-23c6-7dfc-9cdbc5aaf97e
    enabled                 true
    issuer_id               https://mydomain.verify.ibm.com/oauth2
    jwks_uri                https://mydomain.verify.ibm.com/oauth2/jwks
    jwt_type                access_token
    no_default_policy       false
    profile_name            verify
    supported_algorithms    [RS256]
    use_jwks                true
    ```

</Tab>

<Tab heading="Entra" group="entra">

Microsoft Entra ID JWTs use `uti` as the unique identifier claim instead of the
standard `jti`. As a result, you must set `unique_id_claim` to `uti` and
`optional_authorization_details` to `true` to make the authorization details
claim optional in the issued JWTs.

1. Create an OAuth resource server configuration file called `entraid-oauth.json`
   using the environment variables you saved during provider setup:

    ```shell-session
    $ cat > entraid-oauth.json <<EOF
    {
       "issuer_id":                      "${ISSUER}",
       "use_jwks":                       true,
       "user_claim":                     "oid",
       "jwks_uri":                       "${JWKS_URI}",
       "jwt_type":                       "access_token",
       "unique_id_claim":                "uti",
       "optional_authorization_details": true
    }
    EOF
    ```

1. Create an OAuth resource server profile using the JSON file:

    ```shell-session
    $ vault write sys/config/oauth-resource-server/entra @entraid-oauth.json

   WARNING! The following warnings were returned from Vault:

   * user_claim "oid" is not a standard JWT claim - ensure this claim exists in your JWTs
   ```

1. Read the profile to check for correctness.

    ```shell-session
    $ vault read sys/config/oauth-resource-server/entra

    Key                     Value
    ---                     -----
    audiences               [https://localhost:8200/v1]
    clock_skew_leeway       0
    config_id               de81dc66-e00d-23c6-7dfc-9cdbc5aaf97e
    enabled                 true
    issuer_id               https://login.microsoftonline.com/0000000000000-0000-0000-000000000000/v2.0
    jwks_uri                https://login.microsoftonline.com/0000000000000-0000-0000-000000000000/v2.0/keys
    jwt_type                access_token
    no_default_policy       false
    profile_name            entraid
    supported_algorithms    [RS256]
    use_jwks                true
    ```

</Tab>

<Tab heading="Okta" group="okta">

1. Create an OAuth resource server configuration file called `okta-oauth.json`
   using the environment variables you saved during provider setup:

    ```shell-session
    $ cat > okta-oauth.json << EOF
    {
      "issuer_id":                      "${ISSUER}",
      "use_jwks":                       true,
      "user_claim":                     "oid",
      "jwks_uri":                       "${JWKS_URI}",
      "jwt_type":                       "access_token",
      "unique_id_claim":                "jti",
      "optional_authorization_details": true
    }
    EOF
    ```

1. Create an OAuth resource server profile using the JSON file:

    ```shell-session
    $ vault write sys/config/oauth-resource-server/okta @okta-oauth.json

   WARNING! The following warnings were returned from Vault:

   * user_claim "oid" is not a standard JWT claim - ensure this claim exists in your JWTs
   ```

1. Read the profile to check for correctness.

    ```shell-session
    $ vault read sys/config/oauth-resource-server/okta

    Key                               Value
    ---                               -----
    clock_skew_leeway                 0
    config_id                         ef664ac6-9030-0316-7a10-2706c023da14
    enabled                           true
    issuer_id                         https://integrator-c0ff338.okta.com/oauth2/default
    jwks_uri                          https://integrator-c0ff338.okta.com/oauth2/default/v1/keys
    jwt_type                          access_token
    no_default_policy                 false
    optional_authorization_details    true
    profile_name                      okta
    use_jwks                          true
    user_claim                        oid
    ```
   
</Tab>

<Tab heading="Auth0" group="auth0">

Create an OAuth resource server profile using JWKS mode to fetch the signing
keys from Auth0. 

1. Create an OAuth resource server configuration file called `auth0-oauth.json`
   using the previously stored environment variables and both `ES256` and
   `PS256` algorithms recommended by Auth0:

    ```shell-session
    $ cat > auth0-oauth.json <<EOF
    {
      "issuer_id": "${ISSUER}",
      "use_jwks": true,
      "audiences": ["${AUDIENCE_ADDR}"],
      "user_claim": "sub",
      "supported_algorithms": ["ES256", "PS256"],
      "jwks_uri": "${JWKS_URI}"
    }
    EOF
    ```

1. Create an OAuth resource server profile using the JSON file:

    ```shell-session
    $ vault write sys/config/oauth-resource-server/auth0 @auth0-oauth.json

    Success! Data written to: sys/config/oauth-resource-server/auth0
    ```

1. Read the profile to check for correctness.

    ```shell-session
    $ vault read sys/config/oauth-resource-server/auth0

    Key                     Value
    ---                     -----
    audiences               [<audience_address>]
    clock_skew_leeway       0
    config_id               d2838e74-86b6-ef9f-5a8c-c0ff33e095fc
    enabled                 true
    issuer_id               <iss_url_from_auth0_app>
    jwks_uri                <jwks_url_from_auth0_app>
    jwt_type                access_token
    no_default_policy       false
    profile_name            auth0
    supported_algorithms    [ES256 PS256]
    use_jwks                true
    user_claim              sub
    ```

    <Note title="Vault trims trailing slash from issuer URL">

    Vault normalizes `issuer_id` by trimming any trailing slash and casting the
    URL to lowercase while the `iss` claim for Auth0 ends in a slash
    (e.g., `https://...auth0.com/`). The trailing slash difference is expected.

    </Note>

1. Export the `config_id` for use in creating entity aliases.

    ```shell-session
    $ export APP_CONFIG_ID="d2838e74-86b6-ef9f-5a8c-c0ff33e095fc"
    ```

</Tab>

</Tabs>

## Step 3: Create entity aliases

Create an alias for the newly created Vault entity.

Normally, creating an entity alias requires a `mount_accessor` value. If you
provide both an external ID and an issuer that matches your OAuth resource
server profile, Vault synthesizes the correct mount accessor for you when you
create aliases for agentic IAM.

Instead of associating the generated alias with an auth mount, the alias points
to the issuer that grants access for the alias. Vault uses the following format
for the mount accessor synthesis:

<CodeBlockConfig hideClipboard>

```text
oauth-resource-server + _ + <namespace ID> + _ + <server profile config ID>
```

</CodeBlockConfig>

For example, a mount accessor in the `root` namespace would be:

<CodeBlockConfig hideClipboard>

```text
oauth-resource-server_root_de81dc66-e00d-23c6-7dfc-9cdbc5aaf97e
```

</CodeBlockConfig>

<Tabs>

<Tab heading="Verify" group="verify">

1. Create an entity alias for the agent entity:

   ```shell-session
   $ vault write identity/entity-alias         \
     name="jwt-binding-actor"                  \
     canonical_id="${OBO_AGENT_CANONICAL_ID}"  \
     issuer="${ISSUER}"                        \
     external_id="${ACTOR_EXT_ID}"

   Key             Value
   ---             -----
   canonical_id    ef897bd9-0060-1fa4-68ba-65ae5b0747ec
   id              e929f437-f655-45c0-03e7-eb6212dba58d
   ```

1. Save the alias ID to an environment variable. Do not use the canonical ID:

   ```shell-session
   $ export ALIAS_ID="e929f437-f655-45c0-03e7-eb6212dba58d"
   ```

</Tab>

<Tab heading="Entra" group="entra">

1. Create an entity alias for your OIDC app:

   ```shell-session

     name="oidc-app-alias"                   \

     issuer="${ISSUER}"                      \
     external_id="${EXTERNAL_ID}"

<Tab heading="Auth0" group="auth0">

   ```shell-session
   $ vault write identity/entity-alias       \
     name="auth0-app-alias"                  \
     canonical_id="${OIDC_APP_CANONICAL_ID}" \
     issuer="${ISSUER}"                      \
     external_id="${EXTERNAL_ID}"

   ```

<Warning title="You must set issuer on every OAuth resource server alias">

The `issuer` field is **required**. An alias created without `issuer=`
validates successfully but later causes JWT authentication to fail
server-side with `no alias found` / `error looking up entity`.

</Warning>

## Step 4: Create a ceiling policy

Create a ceiling policy to encompass all the possible operations the agent might
perform.

1. Create a policy configuration file called `ceiling-policy.hcl`. For example,
   to restrict access on the `kv`, `pki`, and `transit` plugins:

    ```shell-session
    $ cat > ceiling-policy.hcl << EOF
    # Allow KV2 read and write
    path "secret-v2/data/shared-secret/*" {
      capabilities = ["read", "list"]
    }

    path "secret-v2/metadata/shared-secret/*" {
      capabilities = ["list"]
    }

    # Allow PKI operations
    path "pki/issue/example-dot-com" {
      capabilities = ["create", "update"]
    }

    path "pki/cert/*" {
      capabilities = ["read"]
    }

    path "pki/certs" {
      capabilities = ["list"]
    }

    # Allow transit engine operations
    path "transit/encrypt/app-key" {
      capabilities = ["update", "create", "read"]
    }

    # Allow decrypt
    path "transit/decrypt/app-key" {
      capabilities = ["update", "create", "read"]
    }

    # Optional: allow key metadata read (safe)
    path "transit/keys/app-key" {
      capabilities = ["read"]
    }
    EOF
    ```

1. Write the ceiling policy to Vault:

    ```shell-session
    $ vault policy write ceiling-all ceiling-policy.hcl

    Success! Uploaded policy: ceiling-all
    ```


## Step 5: Register the agent with Vault

Create an entry in the Vault agent registry using the entity canonical ID and
your ceiling policy:

<Tabs>

<Tab heading="Verify" group="verify">

```shell-session
$ vault write agent-registry/register \
    display_name="<ai_agent>-iam"     \
    entity_id="${AGENT_CANONICAL_ID}" \
    ceiling_policies="ceiling-all"
```

For example:

<CodeBlockConfig hideClipboard>

```shell-session
$ vault write agent-registry/register \
    display_name="claude-iam"         \
    entity_id="${AGENT_CANONICAL_ID}" \
    ceiling_policies="ceiling-all"

## Step 6: Validate the token flow

Use the new agent alias to mint and validate token creation in Vault.

<Tabs>

<Tab heading="Verify" group="verify">

1. Create an authorization request file for the `kv` plugin called `kv-token.json`:

    ```json
    $ cat > kv-token.json <<EOF
    {
      "type" : "vault:path_access",
      "path":  "secret-v2/data/shared-secret/test",
      "capabilities": ["create", "update", "read"]
    }
    EOF
    ```


1. Use `curl` to request a token from Verify and save it to an environment
   variable:

    ```shell-session
    $ export AGENT_TOKEN=$(curl --request POST             \
        --variable authz_request=[@kv-token.json]          \
        --expand-data                                      \
        --data 'authorization_details=[{{authz_request}}]' \
        ${ISSUER} | jq -r '.access_token)
    ```

1. Use the minted token with `vault token lookup` to verify your configuration.
   Vault validates the token against the OAuth resource server config profile,
   resolves the entity alias, and returns the default policy:

   ```shell-session
   $ VAULT_TOKEN=${AGENT_TOKEN} vault token lookup
   ```

</Tab>

<Tab heading="Entra" group="entra">

1. Use `curl` to request a token from your OIDC application with `.default`
   scope and save it to an environment variable:

   ```shell-session
   $ export AGENT_TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST \
        -H "Content-Type:application/x-www-form-urlencoded"           \
        -d "client_id=${APP_ID}"                                      \
        -d "client_secret=${SECRET_VALUE}"                            \
        -d "scope=api://${APP_ID}/.default"                           \
        -d "grant_type=client_credentials"                            \
        ${TOKEN_ENDPOINT} | jq -r '.access_token')

1. Use the minted token with `vault token lookup` to verify your configuration.
   Vault validates the token against the OAuth resource server config profile,
   resolves the entity alias, and returns the default policy:

   ```shell-session
   $ VAULT_TOKEN=$AGENT_TOKEN vault token lookup

   Key                 Value
   ---                 -----
   accessor            41s75ML7VIHmb559MGkcYChN
   creation_time       1786737450
   creation_ttl        52m21s
   display_name        JWT Token with Unique Identifier: zgDSchnDlkqnruyuSv50AA
   entity_id           06980be9-4a5c-77f8-258c-7e20aec87a8f
   expire_time         2026-08-14T16:49:52-04:00
   explicit_max_ttl    0s
   id                  <access_token_from_curl>
   issue_time          2026-08-14T15:57:30-04:00
   meta                <nil>
   num_uses            0
   orphan              true
   path                auth/token/lookup-self
   policies            [default]
   renewable           false
   ttl                 52m22s
   type                ent
   ```

</Tab>

<Tab heading="Okta" group="okta">

1. Use `curl` to request a token from your OIDC application with `vault.read`
   scope and save it to an environment variable:

   ```shell-session
   $ export AGENT_TOKEN=$(curl -sS -X POST                    \
       -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded"   \
       --data-urlencode "grant_type=authorization_code"       \
       --data-urlencode "scope=vault.read"                    \
       --data-urlencode "client_id=${OIDC_CLIENT_ID}"         \
       --data-urlencode "client_secret=${OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET}" \
       "${OKTA_URL}/v1/token"                                 \
       | jq -r '.access_token')

1. Use the minted token with `vault token lookup` to verify your configuration.
   Vault validates the token against the OAuth resource server config profile,
   resolves the entity alias, and returns the default policy:

   ```shell-session
   $ VAULT_TOKEN=$AGENT_TOKEN vault token lookup

   Key                 Value
   ---                 -----
   accessor            4940snasDJDxajahdCAAsXSA

<Tab heading="Auth0" group="auth0">

Create a helper script that uses two environment variables (`RAR_PATH` and
`RAR_ACTION`) along with `oauth2` to push authorization requests to the PAR
endpoint of your Auth0 tenant with the RAR claim in `authorization_details`.

The request URI returned by the script is short-lived (30 seconds) and single
use. If you wait too long, refresh the URL, or open it once with `curl` before
using the browser, Auth0 shows an `Oops!, something went wrong` page with
`invalid_request_uri: request_uri not found`.


1. Create `get-rar-auth-token-url.sh` with the following example code:

  @include 'ai-iam/get-rar-auth-token-url.md'

1.Make the script executable:

    ```shell-session
    $ chmod +x rar-authorize-url.sh
    ```

1. Use the script to get a request URI with `vault.read` scope for the
   `secret-v2/data/shared-secret/*` path:

    ```shell-session
    $ RAR_PATH="secret-v2/data/shared-secret" \
      RAR_ACTION="read"                       \
      ./rar-authorize-url.sh
    ```

1. Open the printed authorize URL in a browser to approve the pushed request by 
   signing in as the agent user if necessary and clicking **Accept**.

1. Auth0 redirects you to `http://localhost:9876/callback?code=...` but the
   browser shows a connection error because no server listens on that port. The
   `code` value displayed in the browser address bar is the newly minted token.

1. Copy the `code` value from the address bar and save as an environment
   variable:

    ```shell-session
    $ export AUTH_CODE="c0ff33..."
    ```

1. Use cURL to request an access token from your Auth0 application and save it
   to an environment variable

    ```shell-session
    $ export AGENT_TOKEN="$(curl -s -X POST "https://${APP_DOMAIN}/oauth/token" \
        -d "grant_type=authorization_code"                                      \
        -d "client_id=${APP_ID}"                                                \
        -d "client_secret=${SECRET_VALUE}"                                      \
        -d "code=${AUTH_CODE}"                                                  \
        -d "redirect_uri=http://localhost:9876/callback"                        \
        -d "code_verifier=${CODE_VERIFIER}" | jq -r '.access_token')"
    ```

1. Use the minted token with `vault token lookup` to verify your configuration.
   Vault validates the token against the OAuth resource server config profile,
   resolves the entity alias, and returns the default policy:

    ```shell-session  
    $ VAULT_TOKEN=${AGENT_TOKEN} vault token lookup
    ```

</Tab>

</Tabs>


## Step 7: Validate Vault operations

You can use KV version 2 operations with the minted tokens to validate the
ceiling policies.

1. Enable a KV version 2 secrets engine at the path `secret-v2`.

    ```shell-session
    $ vault secrets enable -path=secret-v2 kv-v2

    Success! Enabled the kv-v2 secrets engine at: secret-v2/
    Create a policy to perform KV operations and link it to the subject entity.
    ```

1. Write a secret to the `kv` plugin as yourself:

    ```shell-session
    $ echo '{"data": {"secret_author": "I am a human"}}' | vault write \
        secret-v2/data/shared-secret/test -
    ```

1. Try to use the original minted token to write a `kv` secret:

    ```shell-session
    $ echo '{"data": {"secret_author": "I am a human"}}' | \
      VAULT_TOKEN=${AGENT_TOKEN} vault write               \
        secret-v2/data/shared-secret/test -

    Error writing data to secret-v2/data/shared-secret/test: Error making API request.
    URL: PUT http://127.0.0.1:8200/v1/secret-v2/data/shared-secret/test
    Code: 403. Errors:
    * 2 errors occurred:
    	* RAR_NO_MATCH: No valid authorization_details claim found matching this request.
    	* permission denied
    ```

    The write fails because the ceiling policy does not allow writes to `kv`.

1. Use the original minted token to read the `kv` secret:

    ```shell-session
    $ VAULT_TOKEN=${AGENT_TOKEN} vault read secret-v2/data/shared-secret/test
    
    Key         Value
    ---         -----
    data        map[secret_author:I am human]
    metadata    map[created_time:2026-06-11T08:04:13.817972Z custom_metadata:<nil> deletion_time: destroyed:false version:2]
    ```

<Note>

`vault kv put` and `vault kv get` use a special type of unauthenticated
preflight check path (`/sys/internal/ui/mounts`) internally to determine
whether the requested KV path is a KV version 1 or version 2 engine.

The request handling flow does not recognize external tokens when routing to
this unauthenticated endpoint and results in an error. This is a known bug,
and you are encouraged to use `vault read` and `vault write` commands to
work around the issue.

</Note>
